A recent study published in 2023 found that 126 pediatric clinical practice guidelines still used race in their decision-making [ ]. Clinical guidelines are meant to standardize care, reduce provider implicit bias, and streamline the management of common diseases. However, incorporating race, which is a social construct, as a proxy for biological processes, is fundamentally flawed; it reinforces bias, discrimination, and vulnerabilities for people of color [ ]. It ignores the historical context in which data have been gathered to justify biased practices that discriminate minority patients as was noted in our findings with lower odds of testing among Hispanic girls. However, we observed a promising trend in increasing frequencies of testing among non-White female children, such that race and ethnicity were no longer significant factors in predicting urine testing in our sub-analysis using the last 5 years of available data (2017–2021). This encouraging trend may be a result of anti-racism efforts in medicine at every level from individual-level interventions to policy-level interventions. In 2020, the American Medical Association House of Delegates recognized racism as a serious threat to public health, to health equity, and a barrier to appropriate medical care [ ]. Future studies will assess whether this trend will continue beyond the study period. Important similarities and differences were observed when we compared our findings to a study that utilized a different data source from 26 US emergency departments in the Pediatric Health Information System in 2009–2019 that analyzed urine testing frequencies among febrile children [ ]. In both of our studies, Hispanic female children had lower odds of receiving any urine testing compared to their White peers [ ], indicating that it is a robust finding. Ramgopal et al. found significantly lower frequencies of urine testing in non-Hispanic Black children compared to non-Black children overall and after stratifying by sex [ ]. Our study also found non-Hispanic Black girls to have lower frequencies of urine testing (Odds ratio 0.75, CI: 0.54–1.03), although it did not reach statistical significance at the 5% level ( p = 0.07). While we observed a differential increase in urine testing frequencies for non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic female patients over time, Ramgopal et al. saw a decrease in urine testing after 2011 that affected females more than males [ ]. Different data sources may account for such observed differences between the studies. NHAMCS is a nationally representative sample of ER visits from all participating US hospitals. Pediatric Health Information System collects data from pediatric-designated hospitals in the US, which means it does not capture care received by children in the hospitals that serve both children and adults [ – ]. Furthermore, overall urine testing frequencies were higher in Ramgopal et al. compared to our findings [ ], which may reflect higher adherence to urine testing guidelines in pediatric-specific facilities. In fact, one study reported higher frequencies of pediatric bladder catheterization at the pediatric-specific emergency departments compared to general emergency departments [ ]. Higher frequencies of urine testing were observed among younger (2–12 months), female children with higher fevers over ≥ 39.0 °C, all of which are important known risk factors for UTI in children according to the AAP UTI guidelines since 1999 [ , ]. Studies estimated the overall prevalence of febrile UTIs in children less than 2 years old to be approximately 7%, with a higher prevalence of 8–8.4% in female children and a lower prevalence of 1.7–2% in uncircumcised male children [ , ]. In fact, a calculator estimating the probability of UTI in febrile infants utilized the following clinical characteristics as risk factors: age less than 12 months, maximum temperature ≥ 39.0 °C, history of UTI, female or uncircumcised male, without other fever sources, and duration of fever ≥ 48 hours [ ]. This validated calculator published in 2018 was found to reduce unnecessary testing, decrease missed UTIs, and reduce treatment delays [ , ]. Our analysis indicates that the providers were using appropriate risk factors supported by evidence-based guidelines to decide when to administer urine tests. Our study has limitations. One major limitation is that the results of the urine tests were not available, which limits our ability to assess the frequency of UTIs in our race, ethnicity, and sex groups. NHAMCS does not capture temperature measured at home at the onset of fever, fever duration, circumcision status, or history of UTIs, which are important risk factors that can influence urine testing frequencies. Although a few reports have questioned the reliability and accuracy of NHAMCS records [ ], the CDC reassuringly reports that the error rate in the NHAMCS database is generally

One major limitation is that the results of the urine tests were not available, which limits our ability to assess the frequency of UTIs in our race, ethnicity, and sex groups. NHAMCS does not capture temperature measured at home at the onset of fever, fever duration, circumcision status, or history of UTIs, which are important risk factors that can influence urine testing frequencies. Although a few reports have questioned the reliability and accuracy of NHAMCS records [ ], the CDC reassuringly reports that the error rate in the NHAMCS database is generally less than 2% [ ]. NHAMCS captures race and ethnicity by various means including medical record extraction, which may be less accurate than direct patient reporting. Individualized data, such as zip codes for each emergency department, were not available, which prevented us from analyzing regional variation on a more granular level and from conducting sub-analyses to test differences in urine testing frequencies in low socioeconomic neighborhoods. Furthermore, we were not able to specifically identify settings that were pediatric-focused or the types and training levels of the treating providers, which may influence the degree of medical testing being conducted. Despite these limitations, our repeated cross-sectional study of a large, nationally representative, randomized sampling survey provided insights into a more generalizable reflection of the care children experienced on a national level during the observation period. Conclusion Our study using a cross-sectional analysis of a nationally representative survey of febrile children presenting to the emergency departments revealed that Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black female patients had lower frequencies of urine testing compared to non-Hispanic White female patients. However, the trends of urine testing for Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black females increased over the study period, and the frequencies now match those of their White counterparts. Further work is necessary to understand whether these trends will impact health outcomes. Supplementary Information Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material. documents.title: AAP clinical practice guideline diagnosis management and prevention of bronchiolitis

chunks.content: Introduction Bronchiolitis is a common acute viral infection of the lower respiratory tract (LRT) in young children with clinical features that overlap with asthma and pneumonia. In 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published clinical practice guidelines for bronchiolitis which recommended against the routine use of inhaled short-acting bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics given lack of evidence that these therapies alter clinical outcomes. Similarly, other international societies have discouraged routine use of these therapies. – These guidelines have motivated quality improvement and de-implementation research that have reported successful reductions in the use of non-recommended therapies. , Further, studies examining large administrative databases also noted large scale reductions in non-recommended therapies potentially indicating widespread guideline uptake. – Because of the overlapping features of bronchiolitis with other common LRT pathology, providers are challenged with ultimate diagnostic assignment of these similar entities, particularly among children <2 years of age. Diagnostic variability and the potential influence of non-recommended bronchiolitis therapies has not been well-studied and may have important implications for understanding current bronchiolitis management practices and database research relying on diagnostic coding. Given the diagnostic complexity of LRT presentations in young children and associated challenges with interpreting existing therapeutic data, we sought to 1) describe temporal diagnostic patterns among children <2 years receiving hospital-based care by exploring the proportion of LRT diagnoses classified as bronchiolitis, asthma/RAD, or pneumonia and 2) explore concurrent temporal changes in non-recommended bronchiolitis therapies (bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics). We hypothesized that apparent decreases in non-recommended therapies for bronchiolitis may be partially explained by diagnostic shifts toward asthma and/or pneumonia. Methods Data Source and Study Design We performed a multicenter, retrospective cohort study assessing inpatient and emergency encounters using the Pediatric Health Information Systems (PHIS) database (Children’s Hospital Association, Lenexa, KS). PHIS is an administrative database that includes encounter-level data from approximately 50 participating children’s hospitals across the United States. Diagnoses are classified by international classification of diseases, 9 th -10 th revisions codes (ICD-9/10) and Clinical Transaction Classification (CTC) codes identify pharmaceutical, supply, laboratory, and radiographic therapies. Encounters are characterized by type and location. This study was reviewed and deemed exempt by our local institutional review board. Study Participants We included Emergency Department (ED) and hospital encounters among patients <2 years with a discharge diagnosis of bronchiolitis, asthma (including reactive airway disease (RAD)), or community acquired pneumonia (CAP) in any diagnostic position presenting to a PHIS-participating hospital. Diagnoses were defined using ICD 9/10 codes ( ) We included diagnoses in any position due to increases in “acute respiratory failure” in the primary diagnostic position for young children with acute respiratory presentations. We excluded encounters with diagnoses of complex chronic conditions (CCC) as defined by Feudtner et al. ( ), hospitalizations with a length of stay >30 days, and encounters from hospitals that did not contribute complete data for the entire study period. For patients with multiple visits before two years of age, we only examined the first visit to try to characterize clinical practices for routine bronchiolitis. Study Definitions and Outcomes We report LRT diagnoses (bronchiolitis, asthma/RAD, and CAP) as proportions. Patients with more than one diagnosis (e.g. “bronchiolitis” and “asthma”) were included in the denominator, but not the numerator for each condition. The primary outcomes were (1) trends in lower respiratory tract diagnoses and (2) trends in bronchodilator (albuterol, levalbuterol), systemic corticosteroid (prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone), and antibiotic use from 2010 through 2022. Hospital encounters included ED, acute care / observation, and intensive care unit (ICU). We treated therapeutic interventions as dichotomous variables (“yes” if a patient received the treatment at least once). We assessed hospital variation in the proportion of LRT diagnoses in the final year of the study period (2022) as a secondary outcome. We performed sub-analyses to describe trends in diagnoses and therapeutics by age (0–12 months and 12–24 months) and by setting (ED, acute care/observation, and ICU). ED encounters were defined as those resulting in ED discharges; inpatient non-ICU encounters were defined as acute or observation level of care only; ICU encounters were defined as those with a billing code for the pediatric or neonatal ICU. Given our observed findings around trends in asthma diagnoses, we performed a post-hoc analysis to explore whether shifts in asthma diagnoses and therapies were associated with revisit rates to the ED and/or hospitalization within 30 and 365 days. These time windows were selected due to the possibility that under-recognition and undertreatment of asthma may have potential short-term (due to lack of bronchodilators and systemic steroids) and long-term effects (due to lack of timely initiation of asthma controller therapy). Statistical analysis We report descriptive statistics as percentages for categorical variables, means (95% confidence interval, CI) for continuous variables, and medians (interquartile range, IQR) for counts or skewed continuous variables. We assessed annual incidence rate ratios (IRR) of LRT diagnoses and therapeutics

diagnoses and therapies were associated with revisit rates to the ED and/or hospitalization within 30 and 365 days. These time windows were selected due to the possibility that under-recognition and undertreatment of asthma may have potential short-term (due to lack of bronchodilators and systemic steroids) and long-term effects (due to lack of timely initiation of asthma controller therapy). Statistical analysis We report descriptive statistics as percentages for categorical variables, means (95% confidence interval, CI) for continuous variables, and medians (interquartile range, IQR) for counts or skewed continuous variables. We assessed annual incidence rate ratios (IRR) of LRT diagnoses and therapeutics over time with negative binomial regression models fitted via Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structured to accommodate the hospitals’ clustering effect. Offset terms corresponding to total encounters per hospital-year were used to model the incidence rates. Calendar year and an indicator variable were used to assess trends and accommodate for the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. Because social determinants of health are associated with asthma prevalence and outcomes, we adjusted for Childhood Opportunity Index (COI; very low, low, moderate, high, very high) in our analyses of diagnostic trends. IRRs were adjusted for calendar year, COVID-19 pandemic effect, COI, and within-hospital variation with hospital clustering to report relative annual rate of change for our temporal data analysis. The same methods were applied to subsets of the data by care location. Data availability for those subgroups might be subject to hospitals’ data sharing policy, leading to a potential smaller sub-cohort of hospitals with complete data; however, we assume that the administrative nature of this missing data results in nondifferential patient demographics and clinical characteristics, thereby not compromising the generalizability of the study results. Type I error was set at 0.05. All analyses were completed using R version 4.4, and the package geeM was used to fit the GEE negative binomial regression models. Results A total of 1,023,745 encounters from 40 PHIS-participating hospitals were included over the study period. Most (62%) encounters were ED only; 28% were hospitalizations (of which 28% were cared for in the ICU), and 10% were observation unit. There were 739,554 encounters (72.2%) with a sole discharge diagnosis of bronchiolitis, 117,252 (11.5%) with asthma alone, and 84,649 (8.3%) with CAP alone ( ). Another 8% of patients had more than one diagnosis, with the most common pairing being bronchiolitis and pneumonia (4% of all patients). Co-diagnoses were most frequent in the ICU (30% of encounters, with 19% being bronchiolitis with pneumonia), and were rare in the ED setting (2.8%, with bronchiolitis and asthma overlapping most frequently (1.4%)). The median patient age was 8 months (IQR 4, 14) and 59% of patients were male. The proportion of LRT diagnoses classified alone as bronchiolitis increased from 55.4% in 2010 to 79.6% in 2022 with an adjusted IRR (aIRR) of 1.022 (95% CI 1.018, 1.025), which signifies an average relative increase of bronchiolitis diagnoses by 2.2% per year. Conversely, sole asthma diagnoses decreased from 22.1% to 6.1% (aIRR 0.918; 95% CI 0.897, 0.939) and sole pneumonia diagnoses decreased from 12.5% to 4.7% (aIRR 0.925; 95% CI 0.913, 0.937) ( a). In the subgroup of 635,725 ED encounters, bronchiolitis diagnoses increased from 56.2% to 84.2% (aIRR 1.024; 95% CI 1.020, 1.029) while asthma diagnoses declined from 25.8% to 7.8% (aIRR 0.920; 95% CI 0.895, 0.946) and pneumonia diagnoses declined from 13.7% to 5.5% (aIRR 0.924; 95% CI 0.911, 0.938) ( b). In the subgroup of 309,596 acute care/observation encounters, bronchiolitis diagnoses increased from 54.8% to 77.9% (aIRR 1.021; 95% CI 1.018, 1.025), while asthma diagnoses declined from 15.9% to 4.5% (aIRR 0.912; 95% CI 0.897, 0.928) and pneumonia diagnoses declined from 10.1% to 3.9% (aIRR 0.929; 95% CI 0.917, 0.941) ( c). In the subgroup of 78,427 patients who received ICU care, bronchiolitis diagnoses increased from 48.9% to 59.9% (aIRR 1.012; 95% CI 1.006, 1.017) while asthma diagnoses decreased from 10.3% to 2% (aIRR 0.887; 95% CI 0.862, 0.912) and pneumonia diagnoses decreased from 12.2% to 2.6% (aIRR 0.883; 95% CI 0.866, 0.901) ( d) In 2022, the proportion of LRT diagnosed as bronchiolitis varied from 65% to 90% for all encounters across participating hospitals. This variation was most pronounced for encounters involving an ICU admission (30% to 87%). Over the study period, bronchodilator administration declined across all encounter settings for all LRT diagnoses from 49.5% to 28.6% (aIRR 0.947; 95% CI 0.936, 0.958). Corticosteroid use decreased from 23.3% to 18.4% (aIRR 0.982; 95% CI 0.972, 0.992). Antibiotic use declined from 13.9% to 10% (aIRR 0.975; 95% CI 0.962, 0.989) ( a). In the ED setting, bronchodilator use declined from 46.6% to 20.1% (aIRR 0.919; 95% CI 0.905, 0.933). Corticosteroid and antibiotic use also declined, but to a lesser degree from 17.9% and 13.3% (aIRR 0.980; 95% CI 0.963,

Over the study period, bronchodilator administration declined across all encounter settings for all LRT diagnoses from 49.5% to 28.6% (aIRR 0.947; 95% CI 0.936, 0.958). Corticosteroid use decreased from 23.3% to 18.4% (aIRR 0.982; 95% CI 0.972, 0.992). Antibiotic use declined from 13.9% to 10% (aIRR 0.975; 95% CI 0.962, 0.989) ( a). In the ED setting, bronchodilator use declined from 46.6% to 20.1% (aIRR 0.919; 95% CI 0.905, 0.933). Corticosteroid and antibiotic use also declined, but to a lesser degree from 17.9% and 13.3% (aIRR 0.980; 95% CI 0.963, 0.998) and 5.6% to 2.1% (aIRR 0.939; 95% CI 0.921, 0.959), respectively ( b). For non-ICU inpatient encounters, bronchodilator use declined 53.4% to 33.8% (aIRR 0.951; 95% CI 0.940, 0.962), corticosteroid use declined from 31.4% to 21.3% (aIRR 0.967; 95% CI 0.958, 0.976), and antibiotic use declined from 26.9% to 14.4% (aIRR 0.952; 95% CI 0.938, 0.965) ( c). Use of therapeutics was more common in the ICU but also declined over time. Bronchodilator administration declined from 65.2% to 57.8% (aIRR 0.989; 95% CI 0.979, 0.999), corticosteroid use from 46.2% to 36.9% (aIRR 0.986; 95% CI 0.977, 0.995), and antibiotic use from 48% to 38.5% (aIRR 0.981; 95% CI 0.968, 0.995) ( d). Diagnosis and therapeutic trends varied by age. For children under 12 months, the proportion of LRT diagnoses classified as bronchiolitis increased from 74.7% to 89.2% (aIRR 1.011, 95% CI 1.009, 1.014) while bronchodilator use declined from 45.6% to 20.4% (aIRR 0.921, 95% CI 0.908, 0.934), corticosteroid use decreased 14.2% to 10.8% (aIRR 0.976, 95% CI 0.961, 0.993), and antibiotic use decreased from 12.5% to 9.1% (aIRR 0.979, 95% CI 0.965, 0.993). For children 12–24 months of age, the proportion of LRT diagnoses classified as bronchiolitis increased from 26% to 60.3% (aIRR 1.059, 95% CI 1.050, 1.068). Bronchodilator usage declined from 55.4% to 45.1% (aIRR 0.973, 95% CI 0.964, 0.982), corticosteroid use decreased from 37.1% to 33.7% (aIRR 0.983, 95% CI 0.976, 0.991) and antibiotic use decreased from 16.2% to 12% (aIRR 0.972, 95% CI 0.958, 0.986). Despite the declining use of bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics in our cohort, 30-day and 12-month revisit rates to the ED and/or hospitalization were essentially unchanged during the study period apart from a decrease in 2020 presumably related to the COVID-19 pandemic ( ). Discussion In this retrospective database-driven cohort study, bronchiolitis diagnoses increased proportionally between 2010–2022 compared to asthma and pneumonia diagnoses for children <2 years treated at a participating US children’s hospital. Concurrently, corticosteroid, antibiotic, and, most notably, bronchodilator use for these conditions in young children has declined. These trends were observed across all hospital settings (ED, non-ICU inpatient, ICU) and in both children < 12 months and 12–24 months of age. Hospital re-visit rates remained stable over time despite declining therapeutic utilization rates. While the exact drivers behind these trends warrants further elucidation, our findings suggest a potential association between therapeutic utilization and ultimate diagnostic classification. Additionally, we observed that the proportion of LRT classified as bronchiolitis varied widely across hospitals in 2022, even after adjusting for COI. This may be driven by local practice patterns rather than true differences in disease prevalence and further demonstrates the challenges around accurate LRT diagnostic assignment in this population. Due to the high prevalence and financial burden of bronchiolitis on the healthcare system, it has naturally become a common target of de-implementation efforts. , , , Investigators have reported successful reductions in unwarranted diagnostics and treatments for bronchiolitis. , , Parikh et al. performed a retrospective study in the PHIS database to evaluate the impact of the 2006 AAP bronchiolitis guidelines on the treatment of hospitalized children with bronchiolitis and found significantly decreased utilization of chest radiography, steroids, and bronchodilators after the guidelines were published. Subsequently, House et al. identified decreasing rates of non-recommended bronchiolitis therapies in the PHIS database from 2006–2019, noting a particular impact of the 2014 AAP guideline publication on immediate and ongoing decreases in bronchodilator rates. While the results of these studies have been encouraging, our group sought to ensure that utilization of these therapies was indeed decreasing in the management of bronchiolitis. Due to the known overlap of bronchiolitis with other LRT disease presentations, we questioned whether reports of declining bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics might be misleading if diagnoses were shifting towards asthma and pneumonia. Contrary to our hypothesis, we demonstrate that as non-recommended therapies have decreased, there has been a substantial increase in the proportion of young children presenting with lower respiratory tract disease who receive a discharge diagnosis of bronchiolitis. These findings raise new questions surrounding the relationship between non-recommended therapies and diagnostic classification. Contrary to our hypothesis, we demonstrate that as non-recommended therapies have decreased, there has been a substantial increase in the proportion of young children presenting with lower respiratory tract disease who receive a discharge diagnosis of bronchiolitis. These findings raise new questions surrounding the relationship between non-recommended therapies and diagnostic classification. Specific to the marked reduction in bronchodilator use and the related decrease in asthma diagnoses, one proposed mechanism is that avoidance of bronchodilator “trials” (as recommended in the 2014 AAP guidelines and other society recommendations) may lessen the risk of attributing observed clinical improvements to bronchodilators. When infants present to the hospital with respiratory distress from LRT conditions, they often receive multiple concurrent interventions (i.e. suctioning, antipyretics, fluid boluses, oxygen support, and observation). If an infant improves following these interventions and received a bronchodilator, they may be labeled as an albuterol “responder” which may lead to a subsequent diagnosis of asthma (with potential exposure to systemic steroids). If, on the other hand, the infant improves but did not receive a bronchodilator, they may be more likely to be diagnosed with bronchiolitis. If true, this explanation has tremendous implications for therapeutic stewardship, as bronchodilator “responder” and asthma labels increase the likelihood that subsequent therapies will be provided. Somewhat relatedly, though we did not specifically address this in our investigation, reduction of chest x-rays (which has been documented for bronchiolitis in the last decade) may similarly decrease the likelihood of misdiagnosing pneumonia and receiving antibiotics. These potential explanations warrant further exploration. In particular, understanding the impact of therapeutic stewardship efforts on rates of asthma diagnoses in young children may have substantial implications on our understanding of asthma epidemiology among this population. One potential concern about a shift away from asthma therapies and diagnoses is that early recognition and appropriate treatment for true asthma might be delayed. However, our post hoc analysis to determine whether hospital revisits increased during this period provides at least some reassurance that undertreatment of asthma in infants and young children is not occurring. Alternative explorations for our findings should be investigated, including the possibility that environmental or epigenetic factors might be impacting asthma trends in young children. Several studies have addressed the overlap of LRT diagnoses and potential influences on resource utilization. Brajcich et al. reported a decline in asthma/RAD diagnoses in 1–4-year-olds between 2010–19 with a concomitant increase in bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia diagnoses. Similar to our investigation, corticosteroid use decreased. Our investigation differs by addressing a younger age group, an extended period (through 2022), broader diagnostic categories and positions (any position rather than primary position), and by evaluating the use of bronchodilators. Nonetheless, our findings echo the notion that diagnostic shifts reported in the literature may reflect changes in clinical practice rather than true shifts in disease epidemiology. Walsh et al. used the PHIS database to demonstrate that the ratio of asthma to bronchiolitis diagnoses increases with age and varies between hospitals. While we also report variability in LRT diagnoses by center, our work differs with a focus on temporal trends in diagnostic assignment and therapeutic utilization. Finally, Cotter et al. evaluated the proportion of children with lower respiratory tract infections who were diagnosed with and treated for community-acquired pneumonia at PHIS hospitals. The authors found that this proportion varied widely between hospitals and that hospitals with higher proportions of treated pneumonia had similar length-of-stay and revisits. Collectively, our work complements these studies that highlight the complex relationship between LRT conditions in young children and demonstrates how the apparent incidence or prevalence of disease may be influenced more by clinical practice patterns than true disease pathophysiology. Our findings may have notable implications for research relying on diagnostic coding to describe disease epidemiology. Future work is needed to elucidate this relationship, particularly the impact of bronchodilator stewardship on a resultant asthma diagnosis. Limitations This study has several limitations. We used administrative data, which does not provide granular clinical information for each encounter, therefore limiting our ability to understand clinical drivers of therapeutic interventions. Furthermore, we are unable to assess the significance of local initiatives at the hospital level (e.g. antimicrobial stewardship programs, creation of clinical pathways, etc.) that could impact our findings. Additionally, the PHIS database includes only encounters at participating children’s hospital centers. Therefore, our findings may not be generalizable to patients treated at other settings such as community-based hospitals or outpatient clinics. Our retrospective study design limited our ability to establish causality for the trend associations observed. Lastly, because our hypothesis was intended to assess the association between therapeutic interventions and diagnostic assignment, we did not analyze diagnostic testing (i.e. CXR use, viral testing, etc.). Shifting

assess the significance of local initiatives at the hospital level (e.g. antimicrobial stewardship programs, creation of clinical pathways, etc.) that could impact our findings. Additionally, the PHIS database includes only encounters at participating children’s hospital centers. Therefore, our findings may not be generalizable to patients treated at other settings such as community-based hospitals or outpatient clinics. Our retrospective study design limited our ability to establish causality for the trend associations observed. Lastly, because our hypothesis was intended to assess the association between therapeutic interventions and diagnostic assignment, we did not analyze diagnostic testing (i.e. CXR use, viral testing, etc.). Shifting patterns of diagnostic testing may also contribute to some of the observed changes in final diagnoses. Conclusions In this multicenter retrospective cohort study assessing children <2 years hospitalized with a LRT disease, bronchiolitis diagnoses have increased while asthma and pneumonia diagnoses have proportionally decreased over the last 12 years. While the mechanism for this finding warrants further exploration, one possibility is that avoidance of non-recommended interventions for bronchiolitis lessens the opportunity for misattributions of causality, i.e. false positive “responses” to bronchodilators. This explanation has substantial implications for the importance of diagnostic and therapeutic stewardship and around our understand of asthma epidemiology. 1. Introduction Immunocompromised individuals are at an increased risk for severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and at a higher risk of mortality after hospitalization due to COVID-19 compared to immunocompetent individuals [ , ]. The risk depends heavily on the extent to which the immune system has been suppressed [ ]. Although vaccinations aim to protect these most vulnerable groups from severe COVID-19, immunocompromised individuals have been shown to exhibit impaired responses to vaccines, including impaired or delayed antibody production [ , ], diminished T-cell responses in some studies [ , ], and greater waning of immunity leading to waning vaccine effectiveness [ , ], and they may not achieve the same level of protection as the immunocompetent [ , ]. This may be due to the immunomodulatory effects of the disease or condition itself or due to treatment with immunosuppressive effects. A primary series of two COVID-19 vaccine doses in immunocompromised populations generates impaired immune responses compared to the general population [ ]. The World Health Organization (WHO) therefore recommended a third dose for all immunocompromised persons [ ]. In Finland, a fourth COVID-19 vaccine dose was recommended at a minimum interval of three months after the third dose in populations at risk for severe COVID-19 in late 2021 [ ]. At the same time, a third (booster) dose was recommended for healthcare workers, older residents in long-term care facilities, and subsequently for all adults [ ]. Thereafter, in 2022–2023, subsequent booster doses have been recommended for those at greatest risk for severe COVID-19. However, specific information on which patient groups would benefit most from booster doses remains limited. With the spread of the Omicron variants of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), vaccinations have provided only very limited and short-lived protection from COVID-19 infections, even in the boosted immunocompetent population. We have estimated that 39% of the Finnish adult population had developed antibody-mediated hybrid immunity induced by a combination of vaccinations and infections during the first half of 2022 and over half by the end of 2022 [ ]. However, data on the development of hybrid immunity in different immunocompromised disease groups are scarce. With the continued evolution of new SARS-CoV-2 variants with increasing potential to evade immunity [ , ], data on the persistence of vaccine-induced and hybrid immunity are required to inform vaccination strategies in this high-risk population. In this study, we examined antibody levels after the fourth COVID-19 vaccine dose in a cohort of severely immunocompromised adults with varying underlying conditions. We aimed to identify patient groups who could benefit from additional booster vaccinations the most. We used Bayesian modeling for the evaluation of factors explaining diminished antibody responses. As the fourth vaccine dose for the immunocompromised individuals was considered their first booster dose, we compared their IgG and neutralizing antibody levels against the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 strain and Omicron BA.1 variant to levels in healthy controls after the third dose (booster). We additionally evaluated the persistence of vaccine and hybrid immunity-induced antibodies up to six months after the fourth dose in immunocompromised individuals with different underlying conditions. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design and Participants The COVID-19 vaccine immunological study is a clinical trial conducted in Finland by the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL) within the well-being services counties of Uusimaa, Pirkanmaa, Kanta-Häme, Central Finland, Päijät-Häme and Ostrobothnia. No investigational products were used. The participants received COVID-19 vaccines, in accordance with the national recommendations, through routine healthcare services. We included two main study cohorts in the study: immunocompromised individuals and healthy controls ( ). For individuals with severe predisposing medical factors affecting the risk of COVID-19, a third vaccine dose was recommended (on 17 September 2021) to supplement the primary vaccination series at a minimum of two months after the second vaccine dose, but due to the short interval, this dose was not considered a booster [ ]. For this group, the recommendation of a fourth COVID-19 vaccine dose at a minimum of three months following the previous dose was given on 22 December 2021 [ ], and it was considered the first booster dose. In Finland, a third vaccine dose was recommended (on 21 September 2021) at a minimum of six months after the primary vaccination series for healthcare workers and the elderly who had received the primary series doses with a short interval (<6 weeks) [ ]. Later, on 26 November 2021, third vaccine doses were recommended for all healthcare workers at a minimum of six months following the second dose [ ]. For the study cohort of immunocompromised individuals, we invited 1440 subjects (aged ≥ 18 years) via random sampling in January 2022. The inclusion criteria were a previous receipt of three doses of a monovalent COVID-19 vaccine (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273 or ChAdOx1 nCoV-19) followed by a fourth monovalent

six months after the primary vaccination series for healthcare workers and the elderly who had received the primary series doses with a short interval (<6 weeks) [ ]. Later, on 26 November 2021, third vaccine doses were recommended for all healthcare workers at a minimum of six months following the second dose [ ]. For the study cohort of immunocompromised individuals, we invited 1440 subjects (aged ≥ 18 years) via random sampling in January 2022. The inclusion criteria were a previous receipt of three doses of a monovalent COVID-19 vaccine (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273 or ChAdOx1 nCoV-19) followed by a fourth monovalent vaccine dose (BNT162b2 or mRNA-1273) by 25 January 2022. A documented previous SARS-CoV-2 infection was an exclusion criterion. The subjects were invited via regular mail and were asked to donate a blood sample at their local healthcare district laboratory after the fourth dose. Any previous laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections were verified from register data. All study subjects were also asked, on their first study visit, whether they had previously received a positive result from an at-home antigen test. Seropositivity with a nucleoprotein IgG antibody test was additionally used to identify previous infections. Study subjects with a known previous SARS-CoV-2 infection were excluded from this study ( n = 58). To evaluate a normal vaccine response, we invited 65 healthcare workers from the Helsinki University Hospital (HUS) in December 2021. Of them, 35/65 had no predisposing medical factors affecting the risk of COVID-19 (as confirmed from healthcare registers) and no known previous SARS-CoV-2 infections, and these were selected as the healthy control group for this study ( ). They received their first two vaccine doses (BNT162b2 or ChAdOx1 nCoV-19) at a dose interval of >6 weeks (median 84, IQR 83–85 days), and they received the third, i.e., the booster dose (BNT162b2), 210 days (median, IQR 198–234) after the second dose and provided serum samples at 36 days (median, IQR 31–42) after the third dose (BNT162b2) in January–February 2022. Their median age was 45 years (IQR 37–56), and 86% were female. We subsequently invited all study participants to a follow-up visit six months after the fourth (median 5.6 months, IQR 5.4–5.9) or third dose (i.e, healthy control group; median 6.0 months, IQR 5.7–6.2) in May–July 2022 ( ). Of the immunocompromised participants, 109/356 (31%) and 5/14 (36%) of the participants in the control group experienced SARS-CoV-2 infection during the follow-up and provided post-infection samples for assessments of hybrid immunity ( ). The participants were considered to have hybrid immunity if they had been infected with SARS-CoV-2 between the first and second study visit (at least seven days before the second sampling). A small number ( n = 38) of the participants who had received four doses of the COVID-19 vaccine at the time when the fourth dose was recommended only to severely immunocompromised individuals had no registered predisposing medical factors affecting the risk of COVID-19. These participants were included in the study as an additional control group, which enabled us to the assess antibody responses after three and four doses in participants with no known predisposing medical factors. We retrieved information on COVID-19 vaccinations from the National Vaccination Register (THL), information on laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections from the National Infectious Diseases Register (THL), and information on predisposing factors for COVID-19 from the Care Register for Health Care (THL), the Register of Primary Health Care Visits (THL), the Special Reimbursement Register for Medicine Expenses and the Prescription Center database (the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, KELA, Helsinki, Finland). 2.2. Laboratory Analyses 2.2.1. SARS-CoV-2 Fluorescent Multiplex Immunoassay We measured the concentration of serum IgG antibodies with an in-house fluorescent multiplex immunoassay (FMIA) [ ] to the SARS-CoV-2 nucleoprotein (N-IgG) and two spike protein (S-IgG) antigens: full-length spike protein (SFL) and the receptor binding domain of spike protein (RBD). We used a threshold of 10 binding antibody units (BAU)/mL for N-IgG seropositivity, resulting in 93% specificity and 100% sensitivity, and thresholds 2 and 3 BAU/mL for SFL-IgG and RBD-IgG, with 100% sensitivity and specificity, respectively. The assay was calibrated to the WHO international standard [ ]. 2.2.2. Microneutralization Assay A live virus cytopathic effect-based a microneutralization assay (MNT) [ , ] was performed to determine neutralizing antibody (NAb) titers against SARS-CoV-2 in subgroups of randomly selected samples ( n = 17–20/risk group). NAb titers were additionally determined for the first 27 samples taken of the 35 healthy controls. We used two SARS-CoV-2 viruses isolated in Finland, between 2020 and 2022, representing the ancestral strain (WT) and the Omicron BA.1 subvariant [ ]. Omicron BA.1 was the most prevalent variant in Finland from the end of 2021 to March 2022, followed gradually by Omicron BA.2 [ ]. The isolation and propagation of the WT strain were performed in African green monkey kidney epithelial (Vero E6) cells [ ]

(NAb) titers against SARS-CoV-2 in subgroups of randomly selected samples ( n = 17–20/risk group). NAb titers were additionally determined for the first 27 samples taken of the 35 healthy controls. We used two SARS-CoV-2 viruses isolated in Finland, between 2020 and 2022, representing the ancestral strain (WT) and the Omicron BA.1 subvariant [ ]. Omicron BA.1 was the most prevalent variant in Finland from the end of 2021 to March 2022, followed gradually by Omicron BA.2 [ ]. The isolation and propagation of the WT strain were performed in African green monkey kidney epithelial (Vero E6) cells [ ] and the BA.1 strain in VeroE6-TMPRSS2-H10 cells [ ] and further propagated in Vero E6 cells for MNT. A tissue culture infectious dose 50% assay was performed for both viruses to achieve a comparable virus concentration among the different strains. Results were expressed as MNT titers; MNT titer ≥ 6 was considered positive, borderline positive when 4, and negative when <4. Borderline positive values were further confirmed by biological repeats. 2.3. Statistical Methods We assessed IgG concentrations in the control group one month after the third dose and used the 5th percentile as the threshold for a normal response. To gain a more comprehensive insight into the variability and distribution of the normal response, we employed bootstrapping, generating 50,000 samples. This allowed us to estimate also the 95% highest density interval (HDI), providing a robust characterization of the response’s uncertainty and distribution. Since most study participants had more than one immunosuppressive condition, a direct comparison of individual patient groups was not possible in this study setting. We therefore used modeling to help identify diseases and other factors that would explain low IgG concentrations one month after the fourth vaccine dose. We utilized a Bayesian gamma regression model with IgG concentrations as the response variable and age, sex, the fourth vaccine product, and the risk group status for various predisposing conditions as explanatory variables. Assuming that only some of the explanatory variables truly impact the IgG concentrations, we used horseshoe priors [ ] for the regression coefficients to induce sparsity in the model estimates. The model was applied separately for RBD- and SFL-IgG concentrations. The reference levels for categorical variables were defined as male for sex, BNT162b2 for the fourth vaccine product and no risk factors for the risk group. We calculated the geometric mean antibody concentrations (GMCs) and titers (GMTs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for IgG and NAb levels, respectively, and compared the concentrations and titers of each subgroup to the control group and the differences in antibody concentrations between vaccine and hybrid immunity groups via the Mann–Whitney test. MNT titers < 4 were assigned a value of 2. We compared the proportions of subjects with a normal antibody concentration (RBD-IgG ≥ 398 BAU/mL and SFL-IgG ≥ 716 BAU/mL), MNT titer ≥ 4 and those who received mRNA-1273 as the fourth dose with Fisher’s exact test. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare antibody levels between different time points within groups. We calculated the Spearman correlation coefficient (ρ) and the statistical significance of the correlation between antibody concentrations and age and between antibody concentrations and MNT titers. The statistical significance level of difference was set to p < 0.05 and adjusted with Bonferroni correction to p < 0.0025–0.025, depending on the number of groups, time points, and antibody/strain specificities in the comparison. Statistical analyses were performed with GraphPad v9 and R version 4.3.2. 3. Results 3.1. Characteristics of the Participants Who Received Four Vaccine Doses In all, 602/1440 (42%) invited subjects participated ( ). Of them, 488 (81%) had received their first two vaccines (BNT162b2, ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 or mRNA-1273) with a dose interval of >6 weeks (IQR 83–84 days) followed by a third dose (BNT162b2, ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 or mRNA-1273) 112 days (median, IQR 90–128) after the second dose. They received their fourth dose 106 days (median, IQR 99–112) after the third dose and provided their first sample for the study 36 days (median, IQR 32–41) after the fourth vaccine dose (BNT162b2 or mRNA-1273). We included these 488 participants in this study ( , ). Half of the participants (264/488; 54%) received BNT162b2, and the other half (224/488, 46%) received mRNA-1273 as the fourth dose. The median age was 64 years (IQR 52–69), and 58.4% were female ( ). The majority of the participants (394/488; 81%) had more than one (IQR 2–4) medical condition predisposing to severe COVID-19 ( , ). 3.2. Impact of Different Factors on Antibody Levels after the Fourth Dose Since most participants who had received the fourth vaccine dose had more than one medical condition predisposing to severe COVID-19 and the patient groups largely overlapped, we were not able to directly compare antibody responses between different patient groups in this study setting. We used the Bayesian

mRNA-1273 as the fourth dose. The median age was 64 years (IQR 52–69), and 58.4% were female ( ). The majority of the participants (394/488; 81%) had more than one (IQR 2–4) medical condition predisposing to severe COVID-19 ( , ). 3.2. Impact of Different Factors on Antibody Levels after the Fourth Dose Since most participants who had received the fourth vaccine dose had more than one medical condition predisposing to severe COVID-19 and the patient groups largely overlapped, we were not able to directly compare antibody responses between different patient groups in this study setting. We used the Bayesian gamma regression model to assess which factors best explain low antibody concentrations after the fourth dose. The results presented in show the lowest estimates of posterior means for regression coefficients explaining SFL- and RBD-IgG antibodies for chronic kidney disease (CKD) (0.479 [0.339–0.741]; 0.490 [0.342–0.787]) and immunosuppressive therapy (IT) (0.612 [0.455–0.845]; 0.652 [0.482–0.940]), respectively. Based on the modeling data, the effects of sex or age on antibody levels following the fourth dose were not significant. mRNA-1273 as the fourth dose (irrespective of the previous vaccine products given) resulted in the highest estimates (1.568 [1.161–2.018]; 1.510 [1.092–1.968]) suggesting better immunogenicity than that of BNT162b2 ( ). However, since there was no information recorded in the National Vaccination Register on whether mRNA-1273 was given as a whole or half dose, we could not reliably evaluate the immunogenicity of the mRNA-1273 compared to BNT162b2 when given as a booster vaccine. The recommendation to halve the vaccine dose when mRNA-1273 was used as a booster was given in October 2021 [ ]. However, it is possible that, especially for those groups where the vaccine response was expected to be weaker, the full dose continued to be used. However, since mRNA-1273, given as the fourth dose, was associated with higher antibody levels compared to BNT162b2, and participants in the control group had not received mRNA-1273, we included only those immunocompromised participants who had received BNT162b2 as their fourth dose in further analyses ( ). In this study, we focused further evaluation of IgG and neutralizing antibody levels on the group of CDK patients and those receiving IT. As with most participants, many of the participants living with CDK had comorbidities that affect immunocompetence. A total of 22/29 (76%) of participants living with CKD were organ transplant (OT) recipients. In this study, we evaluated antibody levels in participants living with CKD or CKD with organ transplant (CDK with OT) but not CKD alone (only seven subjects; ). We did not include the group with OT (without CKD) in the assessment of NAbs because of limited register data available of the time and type of the transplantation. The IT group was large and heterogeneous, i.e., immunosuppressive treatment was combined with various diseases that may have also weakened the immune response. Primarily, we would have selected participants receiving biological drugs (e.g., anti-CD20 therapies such as Rituximab) which are expected to affect antibody-mediated immune responses. However, as these drugs are administered in hospitals, the information is not recorded in the registers to which we had access in this study (the Special Reimbursement Register for Medicine Expenses and the Prescription Centre database, the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, KELA). Since participants living with rheumatoid diseases (RDs) formed a large group within the IT group, and biological drugs (including Rituximab) are used in the treatment of RD, we selected participants of this group to represent those receiving IT treatment ( ). 3.3. Antibody Levels and NAbs after Third Dose in Healthy Controls The antibody levels in the healthy controls ranged between 338 and 4435 BAU/mL for RBD-IgG and 373 and 7036 BAU/mL for SFL-IgG, and the mean concentrations were 1414 BAU/mL (95% CI 1120–1784) and 2168 BAU/mL (95% CI 1713–2744), respectively ( ). We assigned the lower limit of a normal antibody response to vaccination at the fifth percentile of the antibody concentrations: 398 and 716 BAU/mL for RBD-IgG and SFL-IgG, respectively. All controls had NAb against WT and Omicron BA.1, with GMTs of 404 (95% CI 269–608) and 26 (95% CI 18–35), respectively ( ). 3.4. Antibody Levels and NAbs One Month after the Fourth Dose by Disease Groups Here, we assessed the IgG antibody levels in the immunocompromised participants living with (1) CKD (with or without OT), (2) CKD with OT or (3) RD (with IT). We assessed the NAb levels in a small subgroup of participants living with (1) CKD (with or without OT), (2) CKD with OT and (3) those who received IT (without CKD and with or without RD). The majority (93%) of immunocompromised participants were seropositive for S-IgG antibodies after the fourth dose ( ). The percentage of participants with S-IgG antibody levels exceeding the lower limit of a normal response was significantly lower in the

assessed the IgG antibody levels in the immunocompromised participants living with (1) CKD (with or without OT), (2) CKD with OT or (3) RD (with IT). We assessed the NAb levels in a small subgroup of participants living with (1) CKD (with or without OT), (2) CKD with OT and (3) those who received IT (without CKD and with or without RD). The majority (93%) of immunocompromised participants were seropositive for S-IgG antibodies after the fourth dose ( ). The percentage of participants with S-IgG antibody levels exceeding the lower limit of a normal response was significantly lower in the CKD and CKD with OT groups (31 and 18%) compared to the healthy controls ( p < 0.001) ( ). In the CKD and CKD with OT groups, the S-IgG antibody concentrations were significantly lower compared to the control group ( p < 0.0025; ). Within the CKD and CKD with OT groups, SFL and RBD concentrations significantly correlated negatively with age (ρ= −0.438–−0.526, p < 0.025), except RBD-IgG in the CKD with OT group ( ). We evaluated neutralizing antibodies for a randomly selected subgroup of participants with CKD ( n = 20, of whom with OT, n = 16) or IT (without CKD) ( n = 20, of whom with RD, n = 10). In the CKD, CKD with OT, and IT groups, 70%, 63%, and 90% of subjects had NAb against WT SARS-CoV-2 compared to 100% in the control group ( , ). Mean NAb titers against BA.1 were >10-fold lower compared to WT in all groups. In the CKD, CKD with OT, and IT groups, 45%, 38%, and 60% of participants had NAbs against BA.1 which was significantly less ( p < 0.004) than in the control group (100%) ( ). In the CKD and CKD with OT groups, the mean NAb titers against BA.1 were significantly lower compared to the control group ( p < 0.001; ). Levels of NAbs against the WT and BA.1 strains correlated with the levels of SFL- and RBD-IgG antibodies (ρ = 0.448–0.934; ). However, the minimum RBD-IgG antibody concentration generally required to neutralize the BA.1 variant was 200 BAU/mL in the CKD and IT groups. For samples with RBD-IgG concentrations below this, the NAb titer remained negative. We estimated the percentage of participants with NAbs against the BA.1 variant in different study subgroups using this tentative cut-off of 200 BAU/mL ( ). In the control group, all samples had RBD-IgG concentrations ≥ 338 BAU/mL and had NAbs against the BA.1 variant ( ). In the additional control group of participants with four vaccine doses, but no registered medical factors affecting the risk of COVID-19, the mean NAb titers were comparable to titers in the control group with three doses of vaccine ( ). 3.5. Antibody Levels Six Months after the Booster Dose in Participants with and without Infection During follow-up, 109/356 (31%) of the immunocompromised participants experienced SARS-CoV-2 infection ( ). Of the infections, 68 (62%) were documented in the Infectious Diseases Register, and 42 (38%) were identified solely by a >30% increase in N-IgG and/or S-IgG concentrations. Seven participants had hospital-treated COVID-19 disease, and six of them had CKD (including four with CKD and OT), and one had cancer and severe heart disease. The median time from laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection to 6-month sampling was 76 days (range 12–181 days). Since the proportion of participants who received mRNA-1273 (any dose) was not significantly different in participants with or without infection by six months after the fourth dose (44 vs. 71%, 44 vs. 65%, 52 vs. 52%, and 56 vs. 50% for subjects with CKD, CKD with OT, RD, and in the additional control group (with four doses), respectively), we did not exclude mRNA-1273 recipients from the comparison of vaccine-induced and hybrid immunity. Only 14 of 35 participants in the control group (with three doses) participated in the 6-month sampling, and 5/14 had been infected following the third vaccine dose (36%). None of the participants who had an infection in the control group had been hospital-treated. The percentage of participants who had experienced SARS-CoV-2 infection was statistically not different in the immunocompromised and control group (36 vs. 31%; p = 0.769). In participants without infection, the mean IgG concentrations decreased significantly in all groups; 2.0–3.2-fold in the CKD and CKD with OT, 5.8–6.1-fold in the RD, and 4.9–6.0-fold in the control group ( ). The S-IgG concentrations were significantly lower in the CKD and CKD with OT groups than in the control group ( p < 0.0025, ). After infection, the mean S-IgG concentration increased 4.7–9.0-fold in CKD and CKD with OT, 3.7–4.2-fold in RD, and 1.9–2.5-fold in the control group. The increase in antibody concentration (before vs. after infection) was significant ( p < 0.0001) in the RD group

0.769). In participants without infection, the mean IgG concentrations decreased significantly in all groups; 2.0–3.2-fold in the CKD and CKD with OT, 5.8–6.1-fold in the RD, and 4.9–6.0-fold in the control group ( ). The S-IgG concentrations were significantly lower in the CKD and CKD with OT groups than in the control group ( p < 0.0025, ). After infection, the mean S-IgG concentration increased 4.7–9.0-fold in CKD and CKD with OT, 3.7–4.2-fold in RD, and 1.9–2.5-fold in the control group. The increase in antibody concentration (before vs. after infection) was significant ( p < 0.0001) in the RD group ( ). Infection induced increases in RBD- and SFL-IgG concentrations in most subjects with CKD (68 and 79%), CKD with OT (69 and 81%), or RD (84 and 84%), respectively ( ). In the control group (with three does), the RBD- and SFL-IgG concentrations increased after infection in three of the five participants. Six months after the fourth vaccine dose, RBD- and SFL-IgG concentrations were significantly higher in participants who had an infection (i.e., those who had developed hybrid immunity during the follow-up) compared to those without infection ( p < 0.005), except for the CKD with OT group and RBD-IgG in the CKD group ( ). 4. Discussion In this study, we showed that the magnitude of the antibody response after the fourth vaccine dose was sub-optimal, particularly in participants with severe CKD. On the other hand, we showed that infections enhanced antibody levels in most immunocompromised participants. With the emergence of the Omicron variant and the variants that followed, infections have been widespread also in the vaccinated population. Hybrid immunity has been found to provide higher and more durable protection against reinfection and severe disease than vaccination alone [ ]. The data on the immune response to the fourth dose/booster doses and hybrid immunity are limited, especially in disease-specific subgroups, e.g., individuals living with CKD or RD. Our study showed that after the fourth dose, the proportion of participants with a normal antibody response and those with NAb against the Omicron BA.1 variant was significantly lower in CKD and RD groups compared to the healthy controls. Numerous studies have consistently shown that the presence of neutralizing antibodies is a strong indicator of immune protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection [ ]. Consequently, an impaired neutralizing antibody response suggests limited protection. We additionally showed that despite impaired responses to the booster vaccination, the infections boosted the antibody concentrations from what had been achieved with the fourth vaccine dose in the majority of the immunocompromised participants. Further, we conclude that mRNA-1273, as the fourth dose, was associated with higher immunogenicity compared to BNT162b2 in immunocompromised subjects. CKD and RD associated with immunosuppressive therapy have also, in previous studies, shown to impact immune responses to COVID-19 vaccinations. Previous studies have shown overall seroconversion rates being as high as in healthy controls after the primary vaccination [ , , ] but with significantly lower mean RBD-IgG antibody levels, NAb antibody titers (against wt), and lower T-cell responses compared to healthy subjects [ , , , , ]. The third vaccine dose given more than three months after the primary vaccination has been shown in patients with RD to increase the RBD-IgG level, NAb titer against wt/Omicron and T cell response significantly, and compared to healthy controls lower or similar response levels have been reported [ , ]. In patients with CKD, the third dose has been demonstrated to increase the antibody levels, the proportion of participants with NAbs and NAb titer levels, and T cell responses [ , , , ], and seroconversion has been observed in patients who did not respond after two vaccine doses [ , ]. However, in kidney transplant recipients, the rates of response have remained suboptimal [ ]. Due to the significant waning of antibody levels in the months following the third dose [ , ] and the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants with a high potential of immune escape, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control and European Medicine Agency recommended, in July 2022, the administration of the fourth dose to people above 60 years of age as well as to vulnerable persons of any age [ ]. The fourth vaccine dose has been shown to elicit higher antibody levels than the third dose in immunocompromised patients [ ] but lower levels than in the controls in studies with patients on immunosuppressive therapy [ ] and RD [ ]. Few studies have, however, reported NAbs, T cell-mediated or hybrid immunity, and the persistence of antibodies after the fourth dose in patients with CKD and RD. One study reported increased neutralizing activity and T-cell response after the fourth dose in patients with RD. However, in only a minority of the subjects, the level of neutralization against the Omicron BA.2

The fourth vaccine dose has been shown to elicit higher antibody levels than the third dose in immunocompromised patients [ ] but lower levels than in the controls in studies with patients on immunosuppressive therapy [ ] and RD [ ]. Few studies have, however, reported NAbs, T cell-mediated or hybrid immunity, and the persistence of antibodies after the fourth dose in patients with CKD and RD. One study reported increased neutralizing activity and T-cell response after the fourth dose in patients with RD. However, in only a minority of the subjects, the level of neutralization against the Omicron BA.2 strain was above baseline [ ]. We report here significantly impaired antibody levels and NAb titers against the Omicron BA.1 strain after the fourth dose in participants with CKD and with OT. This finding suggests that even after a booster dose, the antibody-based immunity is limited in individuals living with CKD and even more limited in those living with CKD and OT. The progressive waning of antibody levels during the months after the fourth dose shown in this study and the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants with a high potential of immune escape highlight the need for booster vaccinations for people living with CKD. Despite lower humoral responses, vaccination can significantly reduce the odds of severe disease, hospitalization, and death in patients with CKD. However, for CKD patients with persistently poor vaccine responses, and especially for those with both CKD and OT, alternative preventive strategies such as new adapted vaccines or a combined approach of immunization, pre-exposure prophylaxis, and early post-exposure treatment using direct-acting antivirals and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies may be an option. Previous data on antibody response to breakthrough infection in some particular immunocompromised patient groups, especially after the fourth vaccine dose, are scarce. Studies have reported higher antibody levels after hybrid compared to vaccine-induced immunity after two or three vaccine doses in patients with CKD [ , ] and immune-mediated inflammatory diseases [ ]. We show, in this study, that despite impaired antibody responses to the fourth dose, most immunocompromised participants were able to attain a substantial antibody response to infection. At the time of the follow-up of our study (Feb-July 2022), molecular testing was not routinely performed in relation to infections with mild symptoms. Instead, at-home antigen tests were recommended. This practice is reflected in the relatively large proportion of participants (32%) whose breakthrough infection was detected solely via an antibody measurement. Due to the high overall attendance at the follow-up visit, it is unlikely that participants with a known or suspected infection were over-represented. During the follow-up, 7/109 (6%) of infections in immunocompromised participants and 6/19 (32%) in participants with CKD resulted in hospital admission. Our data demonstrate that also a relatively mild or asymptomatic infection can function as a booster in vaccinated immunocompromised individuals. The strengths of our study include the evaluation of factors affecting immune response to the booster vaccination in immunocompromised participants with variable underlying conditions. Also, we compared immune responses to a group of healthy controls with matched vaccine products and a similar schedule for sampling. Because of the limited register data on the dose of the fourth mRNA-1273 vaccine (whole or half) and the greater immunogenicity of mRNA-1273 in comparison to BNT162b2 shown in this study, we performed the comparisons between disease groups after excluding participants who had received mRNA-1273. In addition, we assessed immune responses via antibody levels and NAbs against WT and the variant prevalent at the time of sampling, Omicron BA.1. Neutralizing antibodies are considered a more relevant correlate of protection than antibody levels against severe disease [ , ]. In addition to detecting previous SARS-CoV-2 infections via molecular tests, we also performed N-IgG antibody measurements and asked the participants about coronavirus at-home antigen tests to minimize the possibility of previous infections influencing our results. Our study evaluated humoral immune responses to vaccination and infection, but we did not assess cellular immunity, which is a limitation in our study. Recent data show that despite impaired B-cell responses to vaccination, specific T-cell responses are less dependent on disease or treatment characteristics [ , , , ]. The ability to attain a T-cell response depends essentially on the extent to which immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive therapy affects T cells. Subjects with primary immune deficiencies were found to have robust T-cell responses which can confer protection against severe COVID-19 disease [ , ]. The register-based data used in our study was in part limited as not all details on immunosuppressive treatments were available, e.g., B-cell depleting therapies such as anti-CD20 or immunosuppressive drug mycophenolate mofetil which have been shown to negatively affect antibody responses [ ]. We defined the study subgroups by the underlying disease (ICD-10 codes), notwithstanding the data from previous studies suggesting that the immune status, rather than the disease itself,

immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive therapy affects T cells. Subjects with primary immune deficiencies were found to have robust T-cell responses which can confer protection against severe COVID-19 disease [ , ]. The register-based data used in our study was in part limited as not all details on immunosuppressive treatments were available, e.g., B-cell depleting therapies such as anti-CD20 or immunosuppressive drug mycophenolate mofetil which have been shown to negatively affect antibody responses [ ]. We defined the study subgroups by the underlying disease (ICD-10 codes), notwithstanding the data from previous studies suggesting that the immune status, rather than the disease itself, is responsible for impaired immune responses [ , ]. Since most participants had more than one predisposing medical factor and the groups largely overlapped, a direct comparison between patient groups was not possible, which is also a limitation. During the ongoing follow-up of the study, we will assess T-cell responses and extend the register-based data. The exposure of different population groups to infections may have varied, especially during the first COVID-19 epidemic wave, when containment measures were widely used. The proportion of immunocompromised participants who became infected (31%) during the first Omicron wave in this study was, however, quite similar to the age-standardized seroprevalence of the population (39%) in the Finnish population study carried out at the same time [ ]. Considering that we excluded those participants who were infected before receiving the fourth vaccine dose, the cumulative seroprevalence in the immunocompromised participants would probably have been even closer to that of the general population. The fourth dose of an mRNA vaccine given to immunocompetent individuals four months after the third dose was shown to restore antibody concentrations to the level seen after the third dose but not significantly boost the concentrations [ ]. A longer interval between vaccine doses, or between vaccination and infection, is recognized to increase immunogenicity [ , ]. Very long intervals, up to at least 400 days, between vaccination and infection were shown to result in not only stronger antibody responses but also better cross-neutralization of different Omicron variants. In our study, the subjects had an infection after a relatively short time, within six months of the fourth vaccine dose. Despite this, the infection notably enhanced the antibody responses beyond the levels measured after the fourth dose. Further booster doses have been recommended for immunocompromised subjects, and some may have received up to eight doses by the end of 2023. The long-term benefits of the continued boosting of immunocompromised individuals remain to be seen. In the current epidemiological situation, after many epidemic waves, most people have been infected and many even several times. In light of the current information, it should be critically evaluated whether booster doses are useful to be given repeatedly at short intervals to the immunocompromised or whether vaccinations should be scheduled closer to the start of the expected epidemic wave, e.g., in the autumn season.
